title: How a MOSFET switches: gate charge, Rds(on), and thermal limits
summary: Explore gate drive, load and heat through computed cases with explicit assumptions.

blocks.heading: Pick the variable that is making the device hot
blocks.body: This explorer uses calculated scenarios and answer checks. Start with gate voltage if the switch never gets cool, load current if heat grows sharply with load, or switching frequency if heat grows with PWM rate. These are hypothetical values, not a model of a purchasable MOSFET.

blocks.title: How to use this version
blocks.body: Choose a case in the carousel, predict the result, then use the checks below. There are no sliders or live circuit simulation in this page; the numbers are precomputed.

blocks.heading: The teaching model
rows: 24 V; flat 10 A during each on interval
20 mΩ at an adequately specified gate drive
blocks.caption: Resistive/switching approximation. It omits diode loss, reverse recovery, output-capacitance energy, parasitic ringing and changing load current.

slides.title: Baseline · 10 A, 20 kHz
slides.body: Conduction loss = 10² × 0.020 × 0.5 = 1.0 W. Switching overlap ≈ 0.5 × 24 × 10 × 100 ns × 20 kHz = 0.24 W. Device subtotal = 1.24 W. At the assumed thermal resistance, the one-pass junction estimate is 40 + 1.24 × 40 = 89.6 °C.

slides.title: Double current · 20 A
slides.body: With all other assumptions held fixed, conduction becomes 4.0 W and overlap becomes 0.48 W. Subtotal = 4.48 W; estimated junction = 219.2 °C. That is a model warning to redesign, not an operating point to try.

slides.title: Five times the frequency · 100 kHz
slides.body: At 10 A, conduction stays 1.0 W in this simplified model; switching overlap becomes 1.20 W. Subtotal = 2.20 W and the one-pass estimate is 128 °C. Other frequency-dependent losses may raise it further.

slides.title: Slower transitions · 500 ns total
slides.body: At 20 kHz and 10 A, overlap becomes 1.20 W. The same 2.20 W subtotal appears for a different reason: each transition is longer rather than more frequent.

slides.title: Improved cooling · 20 °C/W
slides.body: With baseline electrical loss of 1.24 W, the estimate falls to 64.8 °C. Cooling changes the path out, not the watts generated in this one-pass calculation.

slides.title: Lower gate voltage · unspecified Rds(on)
slides.body: If the datasheet gives no on-resistance guarantee at your available drive, this table cannot predict the result. Do not interpolate from threshold voltage or pretend the baseline resistance still applies.

blocks.heading: Threshold is the start of conduction, not the drive target
blocks.body: VGS(th) is measured at a specified small drain current. The on-resistance row states a different test condition. For a 3.3 V controller, look for guaranteed performance at an appropriate gate drive or use a suitable driver. Raising drive above the device’s limits damages the gate; “more” is not an unlimited remedy.

blocks.heading: Three quantities that should not be mixed
rows: Gate-drive energy per second; shared by driver and gate-resistance paths
blocks.caption: For the current waveform, use RMS appropriately: I² × duty assumes the stated flat on-current. Do not multiply an already full-cycle RMS current by duty a second time.

blocks.heading: Average drive power can be tiny while peak current matters
blocks.body: Moving 30 nC in 100 ns suggests an average current of 0.3 A during that interval. Moving charge every 50 microseconds can require only milliwatts on average. The real waveform depends on the driver, resistance, device capacitances and Miller charge. Qg divided by current is a rough timing estimate, not a complete switching model.

blocks.heading: Predict before checking
blocks.prompt: With resistance and duty held constant, what does doubling current do to conduction loss?
blocks.explanation: Current is squared: (2I)²R = 4I²R. The model’s 1 W becomes 4 W.

blocks.heading: Read the right datasheet row
blocks.prompt: VGS(th) is 2 V, but Rds(on) is guaranteed only at 10 V. Does a 3.3 V pin establish a low-loss switch?
options: Yes, because 3.3 V is above threshold
No; the required on-resistance at 3.3 V has not been established
blocks.explanation: Threshold only describes the test current used for that threshold measurement. It does not guarantee the on-resistance needed by the load.

blocks.heading: A thermal number belongs to a physical construction
blocks.body: Thermal resistance changes with board copper, package, airflow, heatsink and mounting. Datasheet RθJA describes its test conditions. Short pulses need transient thermal impedance, and linear operation needs safe-operating-area review. A steady-state I²R calculation does not certify either.

blocks.heading: Close the temperature loop
blocks.body: This model deliberately fixes hot Rds(on). In a real estimate, resistance and loss change with junction temperature. Recalculate until the assumptions agree, then verify with an appropriate measurement method and margin. If the result exceeds ratings or has no stable thermal solution, change the design.
